text: Picking a VM size from a gut feeling is probably the single biggest source of wasted compute spend. The good news is you already have what you need to stop guessing: the same metrics pipeline you built out in earlier chapters has been recording real CPU and memory utilization the whole time. Right-sizing is a query problem, not a redesign problem.

Left alone, compute sizing drifts in exactly one direction — up. Someone hits a slow afternoon, bumps the SKU to make the incident go away, and nobody ever revisits it. Do that across a few hundred VMs over a few years and a real chunk of the bill is just paying for headroom nobody is using.

Here's the trap: averages lie. A VM idle at 2% for twenty-three hours and pegged at 95% for one hour during a nightly batch job still averages out to around 12% CPU. Downsize off that average and the batch job starts missing its window. That's why right-sizing leans on percentile utilization instead — p50 for context, and p95 as the actual input, because it captures real peaks without one outlier skewing the whole decision.

Pulling that number is straightforward. In Log Analytics, a KQL query against the Perf table summarizing percentile of CounterValue over a 28-day window gives you p50, p95, and p99 per machine in one shot. In CloudWatch, the equivalent is a GetMetricData call with the Stat set to p95. Run the same query for memory too — and confirm the monitoring agent is actually installed, because memory isn't collected the way CPU is.

Once you have both numbers, the decision is mostly arithmetic. Consistently under roughly 40% on both dimensions for a month or more is a real downsizing candidate — move down a tier or two, not to the smallest possible size. Consistently above 75 or 80% means the workload is running hot, a reliability risk before it's ever an incident. If CPU and memory point in different directions, look for a different vCPU-to-memory ratio instead of resizing uniformly.

The last piece is cadence. A right-sizing pass done once and never repeated decays the same way the original drift happened — new workloads get provisioned generously just to be safe, and six months later you're back where you started. Re-run the p95 query monthly or quarterly, and route any resize through the same change process as any other production change. Next up: once you know the real size you need, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, and Spot — and the real tradeoffs between them.
